response_text:
Here are the most effective ways to get more Google reviews for your business:

## 1. Make leaving a review easy
- **Get your direct review link:** In your Google Business Profile (search your business name on Google or open the Google Maps app), click **"Ask for reviews"** or **"Get more reviews."** You'll get a short link that opens the review box right away.
- **Make a QR code** from that link and put it on receipts, table tents, packaging, business cards, invoices, or a sign by the register.
- **Add the link** to your email signature, website, thank-you pages, and social media bios.

## 2. Ask, and pick the right moment
Most happy customers won't leave a review unless someone asks. Ask:
- Right after a good experience, like a finished job, a compliment, or a repeat visit
- In person, which works best ("It would really help us if you left a quick Google review")
- With a follow-up text or email within 24 to 48 hours. Texts usually get more responses.

## 3. Automate it
- Add a review request to your post-purchase or post-appointment emails and texts.
- Tools like Podium, Birdeye, NiceJob, Grade.us, or features built into your CRM or POS system (Square, Jobber, Housecall Pro, etc.) can send requests automatically.

## 4. Reply to every review
- Thank people for positive reviews. It shows future customers you're paying attention.
- Answer negative reviews calmly and professionally, and offer to fix the problem offline. A good reply can win over people reading it later.
- Businesses that reply tend to get more reviews over time.

## 5. Keep your profile complete and active
Add photos, business hours, services, and regular posts. An active profile gets more views, and more views mean more reviews.

## ⚠️ What NOT to do (it breaks Google's rules and can get reviews removed or your profile suspended)
- **Don't offer incentives** like discounts, freebies, or contest entries in exchange for reviews.
- **Don't "review gate,"** meaning only asking customers you expect to be happy, or screening people first and sending only the happy ones to Google.
- **Don't buy reviews or post fake ones.** In the US, the FTC now bans fake reviews and can fine businesses for them.
- **Don't have employees or family review you,** and don't set up a review station on one device in your shop. Lots of reviews from the same device or location can get flagged and filtered.

## Quick script you can use
> "Hi [Name], thanks for choosing [Business]! If you have 30 seconds, a Google review would mean a lot to our small team: [link]. Thank you!"

**Tip:** A steady flow of reviews works better than a sudden burst. Asking every customer, every time, is the most reliable way to keep reviews coming in.

question: why does my competition show up higher on google maps
response_text:
Google ranks Maps results on three main factors: **relevance**, **distance**, and **prominence**. If a competitor shows up above you, they're probably ahead on one or more of these.

## 1. Distance (you can't change this)
- Google looks at how far each business is from the person searching, or from the area named in the search.
- A competitor closer to the searcher will often outrank you, even if your profile is better.
- **To check:** Search from different spots, or use a rank-tracking tool like Local Falcon, BrightLocal or Whitespark. You may rank well near your address and drop off farther away.

## 2. Relevance (how well your profile matches the search)
- **Primary category:** This is one of the biggest factors. If they picked "Plumber" and you picked "Plumbing Supply Store," they'll beat you on "plumber near me." Look up their categories with a free tool like the GMB Everywhere or Pleper Chrome extensions.
- **Business name:** Names that contain keywords, like "Joe's Emergency Plumbing," rank better. Don't add keywords your real name doesn't have, though. It breaks Google's rules and can get your profile suspended.
- **Complete profile:** Fill in services, products, hours, attributes, description and service areas.
- **Your website:** The page your profile links to should clearly mention your services and city.

## 3. Prominence (how well-known and trusted you seem)
- **Reviews:** How many you have, your average rating, how recent they are, and whether they mention your services. A competitor with 300 reviews will usually beat one with 40.
- **Website strength:** Links from other sites, how much local content you have, and your overall SEO.
- **Consistent listings:** Your name, address and phone number should match everywhere, including Yelp, Facebook, the Better Business Bureau and industry directories.
- **Activity:** Regular photos, posts, answered questions and replies to reviews help a bit.

## Other possible reasons
- **Ads:** Results marked "Sponsored" are paid Local Services or Google Ads listings.
- **Spam:** Competitors sometimes use fake addresses, keyword-stuffed names or fake reviews. You can report them with "Suggest an edit" or Google's Business Redressal Complaint Form.
- **Opening hours:** Google sometimes ranks businesses that are open right now above closed ones.
- **New or recently edited profiles:** Rankings can jump around for a while after big changes.

## What to do first
1. Compare your categories, review count and profile details with the top 3 competitors.
2. Match their primary category if it fits your business better.
3. Set up a simple routine for asking customers for reviews.
4. Make sure your website has a page for each main service and the area you serve.
5. Check your rankings across your whole service area, not just from your own office.

If you tell me your industry and city, I can help you work out which of these is most likely holding you back.

question: can you offer a discount if someone leaves you a good review
response_text:
Not for a *good* review, at least in the US. You can usually offer a discount for *any* review, but there are rules attached.

**What's banned:** Under the FTC's rule, businesses are prohibited from providing compensation or other incentives contingent upon a consumer writing a positive review or a review expressing a particular sentiment. The rule took effect on 21 October 2024, and the FTC can seek civil penalties of up to $51,744 per violation, adjusted annually for inflation. Telling people about the reward doesn't make it okay: violations include cases where the contingency is express or implied, and a reviewer's disclosure of having received an incentive doesn't protect you.

**Watch the wording:** Even hinting counts. Phrases like "Tell us how much you loved your visit!" or "Share your amazing experience for a chance to win!" suggest that only positive reviews qualify for the reward, even if the fine print says otherwise.

**What's allowed:**
- "Leave a 5-star review for 20% off" violates FTC rules. "Share your honest feedback and get 20% off" is compliant.
- You have to clearly disclose the incentive on every review.
- You can't hide the bad ones. If a paid reviewer leaves a 1-star review, you must still display it.
- "Review gating," where you send happy customers to public review sites and unhappy ones to private feedback, is treated as suppression when it hides negative reviews from the public total.

**Platforms have stricter rules:** Even an honest-review discount can break platform rules. Incentivized reviews are banned outright on Google and Yelp, restricted to one specific program on Amazon. A discount for Google or Yelp reviews could get them removed or your listing penalized, even if the FTC would allow it. It's safer to offer incentives only for reviews on your own website, or to just ask for reviews without offering anything.

This applies to the US. Other countries, like the UK and EU members, have their own rules, so check locally if you sell there. For anything high-stakes, it's worth asking a lawyer.
